note: The commentary distinguishes fire that guides or corrects from fire endured as punishment; Augustine discusses the fire that tests works in 1 Corinthians 3 as a possible temporal purification after death, a Christian interpretation that makes the fire's function contested.

The commentary divides hearers between a destructive fate and purification with prayer; the Didache opens by distinguishing a way of life from a way of death, giving an early Christian ethical frame for the divided response.

ref: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses II.20–21
basis: The unconsumed bush in Christian typology
note: In the burning-bush interpretation commonly placed in these sections, Gregory reads the bush's non-consumption through later Christian typology; the section numbering should be checked, but it is a concrete reception of the fire detail central to the commentary.

basis: A governor's brief fire and future judgment
note: Polycarp answers a ruler's fire threat by contrasting a short-lived flame with future judgment; the martyr tradition sharpens the commentary's contrast between Pharaoh's claimed lasting punishment and divine permanence.

The commentary links the body's formation to pasture and contrasts the transient with the lasting; Paul uses sowing to describe a perishable body raised imperishable, making the agricultural image explicitly bodily and eschatological.
The commentary joins embodied formation to the hereafter's lasting life; Paul distinguishes the natural body from the spiritual body in the resurrection, extending that body-and-future connection.
The commentary joins fire with the difference between what is lost and what remains useful; Paul says fire tests each person's work, making fire a test of lasting value.

basis: Fire tests the quality of each work
note: Paul's fire reveals whether work endures, directly extending the commentary's fire, useful remainder, and lasting good into a Christian assessment of works.
The commentary says useful yield remains and receives its due; Paul says the work that survives the fire receives a reward, an explicit ethical form of that contrast.

The commentary contrasts the one who enters fire with the one who performs lasting good; Paul distinguishes burned work from the person saved through fire, complicating the image without equating the passages.
Paul can describe a person whose work burns yet who is saved through fire; that different result makes a useful counterpoint to the commentary's condemned person inside the great fire.

basis: Hidden things brought to light at judgment
note: God will disclose hidden things of darkness and heart-motives, giving a judgmental sequel to the commentary's hidden matter and differentiated outcomes.
The commentary says people prefer worldly life though the hereafter is more lasting; John explicitly contrasts the passing world and its desire with the one who does God's will abiding forever.

basis: The world passes, the doer remains
note: The world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, directly matching the commentary's transient life and lasting good.
Those who hold the eschatological hope purify themselves, a compact Christian parallel to the commentary's purified person oriented toward the enduring future.
The commentary joins remembered revelation to the field's lasting yield; Peter says new birth comes through imperishable seed, the living and abiding word, connecting word and agriculture.

basis: Isaiah's grass applied to human mortality
note: The commentary identifies worldly life with withering pasture; Peter reapplies Isaiah's grass-and-flower image to mortal flesh, showing the Christian reception of that transience text.
First Peter reapplies the grass-and-fading-flower image to mortal human life, a Christian articulation of the commentary's worldly-life-as-grass scene.

The commentary sets the passing world against the lasting better life; Peter's quotation of Isaiah identifies the enduring word with the gospel preached, a Christian interpretive extension of the contrast.
The citation's next verse makes the Lord's word endure forever, matching the commentary's passage from drying life to an enduring word and future.

basis: Faith tested as gold by fire
note: The letter compares tested faith to gold proved by fire, a Christian refinement image for the commentary's corrective fire and enduring value.
The commentary says worldly life is preferred though the hereafter is better and more abiding; Paul explicitly contrasts visible things that are temporary with unseen things that are eternal.

basis: Seen things temporary and unseen things eternal
note: Paul explicitly contrasts the temporary visible with the eternal unseen, giving the commentary's dunya-versus-lasting formulation a close Christian analogue.
The commentary joins crop, good work, and a remaining share; Paul says God supplies seed and increases the harvest of righteousness, applying agricultural yield to generous action.
The commentary's magicians prostrate and choose God over Pharaoh; Paul's named Egyptian opponents resist Moses and the truth, preserving the opposite outcome in Christian memory.
The letter gives traditional names to men who opposed Moses, a Christian reception of the Egyptian-magician conflict that the commentary brings into the Pharaoh scene.

basis: Times and seasons fixed by the Father's authority
note: Jesus withholds the times and seasons as the Father's own domain, complementing the commentary's hidden temporal decree without claiming the same formulation.

basis: Prayers ascending as a memorial before God
note: Cornelius's prayers and alms rise as a memorial before God, a specific Christian use of prayer and remembrance that complements the commentary's li-dhikri.

basis: Moses read in synagogues every Sabbath
note: Acts describes Moses as publicly read in every city from ancient generations, a Christian witness to the continuing recitation of the Mosaic writings invoked by the commentary.
Former practitioners publicly burn their magical books after confession, a later Christian scene of renouncing magic that complements the commentary's converted magicians without repeating its plot.

basis: Moses sees the bush in flame
note: The commentary makes the distant fire the place of Moses' encounter; Stephen retells the bush appearing to Moses in a flame, preserving that same scene in Christian memory.
Acts explicitly retells an angel appearing to Moses in a flame of a bush in the wilderness, preserving the scene around which the commentary gathers call and guidance.
The commentary joins the fire to selection and a new path; Stephen's retelling has God send Moses to bring Israel out, spelling out the rescue mission that follows the fire.

basis: The bush appearance and Moses's sending
note: Stephen calls Moses the man sent by God as ruler and deliverer through the angel who appeared in the bush; it joins election at the fire to opposition from Egypt.
Grace is given to each according to the measure of Christ's gift, a Christian individual-allotment image relevant to the commentary's move from measuring to portioning.

basis: Set apart from the womb and called
note: Paul describes being set apart from his mother's womb and called by grace, a Christian counterpart to formed life that is also chosen for a task.
Paul personifies Scripture as announcing blessing beforehand to Abraham, a Christian rereading that makes Abraham a recipient of prior scriptural proclamation.
The commentary calls the present world a field and the hereafter the more lasting yield; Paul contrasts sowing to flesh with sowing to Spirit and names eternal life as the harvest.

basis: Sowing for decay or eternal life
note: Sowing to flesh reaps corruption while sowing to Spirit reaps eternal life, translating the commentary's worldly and afterlife fields into a moral agricultural choice.
The commentary says cultivated land grows and leaves a share; Paul urges perseverance in doing good because the harvest comes in due season.

basis: Doing good and reaping in due season
note: The promise that persistent good will reap at the proper time supplies a Christian counterpart to the commentary's lasting good that remains after the transient growth goes.

basis: Cleansed bodies and drawing near in worship
note: The faithful draw near with hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed, joining purification and worship as the commentary joins tazkiya, name-remembrance, and prayer.
Moses refuses the status of Pharaoh's daughter's son, a specific Christian reading of the choice the commentary places beside Pharaoh's transient rule.
Moses chooses ill-treatment with God's people rather than sin's temporary enjoyment, closely matching the commentary's preference between the near worldly life and what lasts.

The commentary uses the magicians' rejection of Pharaoh's temporary authority and the preference for what lasts; Hebrews says Moses chose reproach over Egypt's treasures because he looked to the reward, applying that choice to Moses himself.

basis: Egyptian treasure weighed against a future reward
note: Moses values reproach above Egypt's treasures because he looks to recompense; the verse gives the commentary's choice and permanence an explicitly Mosaic Christian form.

basis: Abraham obeys a call into an unknown destination
note: Abraham obeys and goes out without knowing his destination, a Christian counterpart to the commentary's Abrahamic trust, calling, and path imagery.

basis: Receiving an unshakable kingdom and offering worship
note: The community receives an unshakable kingdom and offers acceptable worship with awe, a Christian framing for the commentary's worship and permanence after transient life.
Hebrews names God a consuming fire in a worship context, a concise Christian meeting of the commentary's divine fire, awe, and praise.

basis: Praise offered with lips confessing God's name
note: The community continually offers praise to God as the fruit of lips acknowledging the name, a direct Christian liturgical counterpart to the commentary's name, praise, and prayer.
All creatures are exposed before the God to whom account is given, a direct Christian formulation for the commentary's God who knows what is open and concealed.
The commentary contrasts vegetation that becomes refuse with what remains useful; Hebrews compares land drinking frequent rain and yielding a useful crop, an unusually close rain-and-yield image.

basis: Rain-drinking ground that yields a useful crop
note: Ground receives rain and produces a crop useful to its cultivators, a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's worked field that grows and remains beneficial.

The commentary says untended growth dries and is carried away while useful yield remains; Hebrews contrasts thorns with fruitful land and ends the barren plot in burning, making the moral sorting sharper.
Ground producing thorns is rejected and ends in burning; it gives the commentary's neglected weed, field, and fire a sharply opposed agricultural outcome.

basis: Abraham and the priest of God Most High
note: Hebrews names Melchizedek priest of God Most High in his encounter with Abraham, a Christian reuse of the highness title alongside Abraham; it is a title-and-scene meeting rather than a shared story.
The commentary says the world-life is also called a flower and does not last; James compares the rich person to a flower brought low, attaching that image to worldly status.
The commentary's pasture dries and the world's flower passes; James describes the sun scorching the flower until it falls, making heat the specific cause of fading.

basis: The rich person fading like grass's flower
note: James uses scorched grass and fallen flower for the rich person's passing career, a specific Christian application of the commentary's worldly-life-as-drying-vegetation image.

basis: Not a forgetful hearer but a doer
note: James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the persevering doer of the perfect law, directly pairing the commentary's reminder with its division between response and avoidance.

basis: Draw near, cleanse hands, and purify hearts
note: James pairs drawing near to God with cleansing and a divided heart's purification, directly meeting the commentary's tazkiya and worshipful response.

The commentary says the cultivated field's yield grows and leaves a share; James pictures a farmer patiently waiting for the earth's precious crop through early and late rains, extending the agricultural image to expectation.

The commentary opens its second movement with a promise of recitation without forgetting; Jesus says the Spirit will remind the disciples of his words, a distinct Christian promise of remembered revelation.

basis: Fruit-bearing branches pruned for greater fruit
note: The grower prunes fruitful branches so they bear more fruit, supplying the corrective cultivation missing from the dried-and-burned branch image already developed by the commentary.
The commentary says good work grows from a cultivated field and leaves a remainder; Jesus says those who abide in him bear much fruit, making lasting yield depend on remaining in him.

The commentary links dried growth to loss and fire to two outcomes; Jesus describes an unfruitful branch drying up and being thrown into the fire, a specific but differently framed plant-and-fire image.

basis: Unfruitful branch dries and is thrown into fire
note: A branch not abiding is dried, gathered, and burned, a concentrated Christian image for the commentary's dried vegetation and fire-bound outcome.
The commentary links the remembered word with lasting good; Jesus says his words abide in disciples who abide in him, joining remembered instruction to the fruit-bearing image.

basis: Hearing the word passes from death into life
note: The one who hears and believes has eternal life and has crossed from death to life, a Christian response-to-reminder counterpart to the commentary's fire-bound non-life and purified alternative.

basis: Jesus says Moses wrote of him
note: Jesus grounds his appeal in Moses's writing, a Christian interpretation of Mosaic pages that belongs beside the commentary's appeal to Moses as an earlier written authority.

basis: Following the light on the way to life
note: Jesus promises that followers of the world's light will not walk in darkness but have life's light; it is a Christian path-and-light counterpart to the commentary's fire sought for guidance.

The commentary compares flood foam with the refuse of vegetation and contrasts it with useful remainder; Jude calls false teachers wild sea waves foaming up their shame, giving foam a specific image of worthless discharge.

basis: Saving someone by snatching them from fire
note: Jude distinguishes rescuing people from fire from sharing their defilement, a concrete Christian complement to the commentary's concern with approaching versus entering fire.
The commentary contrasts preferred worldly life with the lasting hereafter; Jesus ends the rich fool's story by contrasting stored earthly goods with being rich toward God.

basis: Present goods reversed into future comfort and anguish
note: Abraham contrasts the rich man's received good things in life with his later anguish and Lazarus's comfort, closely framing the commentary's worldly preference and later permanence.
Jesus commands the meal to be done in his remembrance; its explicit liturgical remembering is a Christian parallel to the commentary's fire-side prayer for remembrance.
The commentary moves from recited revelation to pasture and a field of outcomes; Jesus identifies the seed as God's word, joining the reminder and agricultural imagery in one interpretation.
The commentary divides hearers and describes cultivated land yielding a lasting share; Jesus says the good soil hears the word, holds it fast, and bears fruit with endurance.

basis: The book of Moses at the bush
note: Jesus identifies the bush episode as a passage in the book of Moses, directly joining the commentary's final Moses pages to its opening fire encounter.

basis: The day and hour known only to the Father
note: Jesus says the decisive day and hour are known to the Father alone, a close Christian analogue to the commentary's divinely concealed hour.

The commentary describes the person in the great fire as neither dying nor living; Mark's Gehenna saying depicts fire that is not quenched, a specific shared punishment image with a different emphasis.

basis: Christian citation of undying worm and unquenched fire
note: Mark preserves Isaiah's image for Gehenna, making an explicit Christian counterpart to the commentary's fire in which ordinary death does not bring release.

basis: A ruler's limited power over life
note: Jesus distinguishes people who can kill only the body from God who judges finally; this clarifies the commentary's assertion that Pharaoh rules only this worldly life while God is more enduring.
The commentary says dry growth is swept away while useful yield remains; Jesus' parable keeps weeds and wheat until harvest, when the weeds are bound for burning and wheat stored.
The parable preserves wheat while gathering weeds for burning, closely pairing the commentary's useful field, rejected vegetation, division, and fire.
The commentary uses dead pasture for the failing worldly life; Jesus interprets weeds as evil and their burning as the end of the age, a specific but differently mapped agricultural judgment.

basis: Weeds gathered and burned at the age's end
note: Jesus explains the weed-and-fire image as an end-time sorting, a necessary interpretive continuation of the field scene and the commentary's future fire.

basis: Righteous shining in their Father's kingdom
note: The righteous shine in the kingdom after the furnace judgment, a Christian continuation that meets the commentary's high degrees and lasting reward.

The commentary sets the one in fire against the one purified and praying; Jesus' judgment scene ends with two groups sent to eternal punishment or eternal life, a direct afterlife counterpart to the divided fates.
The final separation gives the two groups eternal punishment or eternal life, a Christian counterpart to the commentary's split between fire and the purified, praying person.

basis: Wheat gathered and chaff burned with unquenchable fire
note: The coming judge stores wheat but burns chaff, tightly combining the commentary's useful remainder, agricultural waste, human division, and great fire.
The commentary says people put worldly life first though another life lasts; Jesus warns against storing treasure on earth, making present attachment the explicit choice at issue.
The commentary calls the hereafter better and more abiding; Jesus directs disciples to store treasure in heaven, giving a concrete alternative to earthly preference.

basis: Prayer to the Father who sees in secret
note: Jesus places prayer in the hidden room before the Father who sees in secret, directly combining the commentary's prayer-for-remembrance with its hidden divine knowledge.
The opening petition of the Lord's Prayer hallows the Father's name, an explicit Christian prayer counterpart to the commentary's remembering the Lord's name and praying.
The broad gate and way end in destruction, providing a Christian path-and-outcome counterpart to the commentary's guidance, choice, and fire.
The difficult way leads to life and few find it, sharpening the commentary's sought guidance and its contrast between life-oriented response and loss.
The commentary says the reminder divides people by their response; Jesus compares the one who hears and does his words to a builder, tying reception of instruction to the outcome of a house.

basis: Hearing and doing words builds on rock
note: The person who hears Jesus's words and does them is likened to a wise builder, a Christian response-to-reminder counterpart to the commentary's beneficial admonition.
The commentary's flood carries off refuse while useful matter remains; the house built on rock stands through rain, flood, and wind, a close counter-image of what endures the waters.

basis: Rain and floods fail to overthrow the founded house
note: Rain, flood, and wind strike the rock-founded house but it remains, directly meeting the commentary's flood and the contrast between what goes away and what remains.

The commentary distinguishes those who remember from those who avoid the reminder; Jesus contrasts the hearer who does not act with the wise builder, specifying failure to act as the decisive difference.

basis: Hearing without doing builds on sand
note: The hearer who does not act on the words builds on sand, providing a counterpart to the commentary's person who avoids the reminder.
The commentary's flood removes what cannot last; Jesus' flood causes the ungrounded house to collapse, dramatizing the consequence of rejecting the words heard.

basis: Flood destroys the house with no foundation
note: Rain and floods bring a great fall to the sand-founded house, completing the commentary's water-borne testing and opposed human outcomes.

basis: Every knee bends at the exalted name
note: The universal bending of knees at the name gives a Christian liturgical analogue to the commentary's prostration and exalted name, with a different christological setting.

basis: A name highly exalted above every name
note: God highly exalts a name above every name, a Christian reapplication of name-and-highness that is relevant to the commentary's praise of the highest Lord but does not share its speaker.

basis: The song of Moses as praise
note: The heavenly worshippers sing the song of Moses in praise of God's great works, a Christian liturgical meeting of Moses, praise, and enduring divine rule.

basis: Lake of fire called the second death
note: Revelation names the fiery lake the second death; its wording supplies a deliberate Christian contrast to the commentary's fire in which death and life are both denied.
Revelation's renewed world abolishes death, mourning, and pain; its eschatological endpoint gives a Christian counter-horizon to the commentary's fire where neither death nor life occurs.
The commentary says the one in fire neither dies nor lives; Revelation depicts people seeking death without finding it, a close suspended-death image in a different apocalyptic scene.

basis: People seek death but death flees
note: In Revelation's torment people long to die yet cannot find death; this is a particularly close formulation beside the commentary's neither-dying-nor-living fire.

basis: A measure of faith allotted by God
note: God assigns each person a measure of faith, supplying another specific Christian use of divinely apportioned measure beside the commentary's qadar imagery.

The commentary says the cultivated field's yield is lasting good; Paul describes those who persist in good work seeking immortality as receiving eternal life, an ethical counterpart to that lasting yield.

The commentary contrasts the painful fire of one fate with the better enduring hereafter; Paul says present sufferings are not comparable to the glory to be revealed, giving a Christian formulation of present and future value.
Paul uses a potter making vessels for different purposes, joining divine fashioning to differentiated allotment in the way the commentary connects creation and choice.

basis: Mortal death and resurrection unto life
note: Another brother contrasts death at human hands with hope of resurrection and tells the tyrant he has no resurrection to life; it is a pointed counter-formulation to neither dying nor living in the fire.

basis: A tyrant ends present life, God raises to lasting life
note: A tortured brother tells the king that he may dismiss them from present life but the King of the world will raise them to everlasting life, closely meeting Pharaoh's threat and the better enduring life.

basis: A restored corpus of revealed books
note: Ezra's scribes complete ninety-four books after the law's loss, a Jewish apocalyptic meditation on preserving and differentiating former sacred writings.

basis: Furnace of torment opposed to a place of rest
note: The apocalyptic vision displays the furnace of Gehenna opposite a place of rest, a Jewish eschatological pairing for the commentary's fire and enduring differentiated outcome.

basis: Abraham's early confrontation with household idols
note: The opening idol episodes are commonly cited for Abraham's testing and rejection of Terah's idols and fire-associated separation; the exact internal sequence should be verified, but it is a specific expansion of the commentary's anti-idolatry Abraham.
The Talmud's statement that Moses wrote his book is a Jewish reception of Mosaic textual authority relevant to the commentary's named pages of Moses.

basis: Righteous enjoying divine radiance in the world to come
note: The Talmud's world-to-come scene gives the righteous crowns and enjoyment of divine radiance, a Jewish interpretive counterpart to enduring high degrees rather than temporary worldly life.

The commentary reads Moses' fire as guidance rather than punishment; this midrash reads the unconsumed bush as Israel suffering in Egypt without being destroyed, shifting the sign toward collective endurance.

The commentary invokes Abraham's request for distance from idols; this midrash's idol-breaking account portrays Abraham actively rejecting his father's idols, making the cited prayer a narrative practice.

basis: Abraham's idol challenge and the furnace
note: The midrash has Abraham reject idols and be cast into Nimrod's furnace, a Jewish expansion that tightly joins the commentary's Abrahamic anti-idolatry with its repeated fire scenes.

These verses are commonly associated with young Abram's recognition of the earth's error in following carved images and his prayer for deliverance; exact wording and division should be verified, but the link is a specific Jewish precursor to the commentary's anti-idolatry Abraham.
The commentary recalls Abraham's plea against idolatry; Jubilees expands his break with his father's idol-making household, giving an early Jewish narrative counterpart to the separation.
The Mishnah applies Deuteronomy's warning to the deliberate forgetting of a learned word; it is a Jewish interpretive intensification of the commentary's not-forgetting motif.

The commentary says people prefer present worldly life despite the better hereafter; the Mishnah likens this world to a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation, turning preference into a practical orientation.

basis: This world as corridor before the world to come
note: Rabbi Jacob calls this world a vestibule before the world to come, a precise rabbinic frame for the commentary's worldly life versus the later, enduring life.

The commentary joins cultivated good work to lasting reward and says the hereafter is better than this life; Avot compares one hour of repentance and good deeds here with the world to come, and one hour of its bliss with all this life.

basis: Good deeds here and bliss in the world to come
note: The saying weighs repentance and good deeds in this world together with the incomparable bliss of the world to come, closely mapping the commentary's earthly choice and better permanence.
The commentary joins bodily creation to divine measuring; Sirach says God made humans from earth and allotted them numbered days, bringing formation and measure together.

basis: Gold tested in fire and the righteous in humiliation
note: Sirach's fire-testing of gold supplies a Jewish wisdom formulation for the commentary's corrective fire, without making it identical to the punitive fire.

basis: Elijah's prayer to the God of Abraham at a fire contest
note: Elijah invokes the God of Abraham before the altar fire and asks that Israel know God and his servant; it joins fire, Abraham, divine name, and a public contest of allegiance.
The fire of YHWH falls on Elijah's offering, furnishing a Hebrew-Bible fire scene whose purpose is revelation and correction rather than the destruction of a condemned person.

basis: People fall on their faces and confess God
note: After the fire the people prostrate themselves and confess YHWH as God, a close narrative meeting of fire, praise, and bowing with the commentary's magicians' prostration.
At the temple dedication fire descends and God's glory fills the house, a further biblical scene in which fire marks divine presence rather than entry into punitive fire.

basis: Bowing and praise after the fire
note: Seeing the fire and glory, Israel bows and gives thanks for God's enduring steadfast love; it closely combines the commentary's fire, praise, prostration, and permanence.

basis: God reveals a secret to prophetic servants
note: Amos says God discloses the divine secret to prophets, a specific prophetic counterpart to the commentary's hidden matter becoming disclosed guidance.

basis: Many purified and refined, while the wicked do not understand
note: The end-time division has many made pure and refined while the wicked continue blindly; it closely meets the commentary's tazkiya, reminder, and divided response.

The commentary divides people between fire and purification and contrasts their ultimate fates; Daniel says sleepers in the dust awaken to everlasting life or shame, a specific scriptural division after death.
Daniel's awakening divides people between everlasting life and enduring disgrace, furnishing a biblical future horizon for the commentary's high ranks and great fire.

basis: Those guiding many to righteousness shine forever
note: The wise shine and those who turn many to righteousness shine like stars forever, a biblical counterpart to guidance, high degrees, and lasting reward.

basis: Words shut up and book sealed until the end
note: Daniel is told to close the words and seal the book until the time of the end, a direct biblical combination of hidden end-time knowledge and written pages.

basis: God knows and reveals hidden things
note: Daniel says God reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in darkness, closely meeting the commentary's God who knows what is open and concealed.

basis: Refusal to worship under a king's fire threat
note: The Judeans refuse the king's gods even when a furnace is threatened; the scene closely meets the commentary's prostrating magicians who reject a tyrant's finite authority.

The commentary contrasts punitive fire with the fire at which Moses receives guidance; Daniel's furnace contains a fourth figure beside the three condemned men, making divine presence visible within lethal fire.

basis: Entrants into fire who are unharmed
note: The king sees the furnace's entrants walking unhurt; its outcome stands in deliberate tension with the commentary's person who enters the great fire and neither dies nor lives.
The commentary distinguishes one who enters fire from Moses approaching it safely; Daniel's men emerge without bodily harm, a related reversal of fire's destructive action.

basis: The Most High gives kingdoms to whom he wills
note: Daniel says the Most High rules human kingdoms and gives them as he chooses, directly contesting Pharaoh's self-exalting authority and joining highness to election.

basis: A humbled king praises the Most High
note: After his humiliation, the king blesses and honors the Most High whose dominion endures; it reverses the commentary's tyrannical high claim with praise and lasting rule.

basis: Holy ones of the Most High possess an everlasting kingdom
note: The holy ones of the Most High receive and possess the kingdom forever, a direct biblical meeting of highestness, elevated status, and permanence.

basis: Everlasting kingdom given to the people of the Most High
note: All dominions serve the holy people whose kingdom endures, answering the commentary's tyrant's temporary rule with lasting high rule under God.

basis: A written Torah copy read throughout life
note: The king must write a Torah copy and keep it for continual reading and fear of God, a precise model of page, remembrance, obedience, and durable instruction.

basis: A harvested sheaf deliberately left for others
note: The forgotten sheaf must remain for the resident alien, orphan, and widow, concretely illuminating the commentary's claim that a field's produce has a due share left behind.

The commentary says God knows what is open and hidden and places a nearly hidden event in Moses' scene; Moses distinguishes secret things belonging to God from revealed things given to Israel, marking a related boundary without equating the subjects.
The secret belongs to God while what is revealed is for communal obedience, a precise Torah counterpart to the commentary's hidden divine matter and disclosed teaching.

basis: Life and good set against death and evil
note: Moses sets life and good before Israel against death and evil, a Torah form of the two human outcomes the commentary traces from reminder through fire and purification.

The commentary contrasts preferring worldly life with the better lasting hereafter; Moses urges Israel to choose life by covenant loyalty, a related choice formula whose immediate setting is life in the land.
The commentary repeats Arabic ḥayāt for worldly life; Moses' choice formula uses Hebrew ḥayyîm, a cognate for life, though here it means covenantal life in the land.
The call to choose life gives explicit Mosaic form to the commentary's language of preference and its contrast between the near life and what truly endures.

basis: Arabic hayat and Hebrew hayyim in the command to choose life
note: Beyond the existing choice motif, the Hebrew command choose hayyim and the commentary's hayat are cognate life terms; the verse grounds its life-choice in an explicit Semitic formulation.
The commentary describes a reminder publicly offered and recited; Moses sets the law's public reading at the seven-year festival, giving the reading a recurring communal setting.
The commentary describes revealed speech being recited and offered as reminder; Moses orders the law read publicly before all Israel, giving a communal scriptural counterpart.
The commentary divides hearers between those who fear and remember and those who turn away; the assembly is to hear the law, learn, and fear the Lord, including children and sojourners.
The commentary's fearful hearer remembers the reminder; Moses says future generations must hear and learn to fear God all their days in the land.

basis: Write and teach the song as a witness
note: God tells Moses to write a song, teach it, and put it in Israel's mouths; it supplies a Mosaic written-and-remembered form for the commentary's recitation and warning.

basis: A song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
note: The divinely given song will not be forgotten from descendants, a particularly close biblical analogue to the commentary's not-forgetting and enduring instruction.

basis: Moses completes writing Torah in a book
note: The verse explicitly depicts Moses finishing the words of Torah in a book, the clearest canonical textual counterpart to Moses's pages in 87:19.

basis: The Torah book kept as witness
note: The written Torah is placed beside the ark as a witness, giving the commentary's named Mosaic pages a preserved and judicial function.

The commentary joins reminder and guidance to rain-fed pasture; in Moses' song, his teaching descends like rain and his speech like dew, bringing recited instruction and the section's water imagery together.

basis: Teaching falling like rain on grass
note: Moses compares teaching to rain, dew, and showers on tender grass, directly connecting the commentary's reminder to its water-and-pasture landscape.

basis: Proclaiming the divine name and ascribing greatness
note: Moses announces that he will proclaim YHWH's name and ascribe greatness to God, a close Torah counterpart to the commentary's praise of the exalted Lord and mention of the name.

The commentary moves from revealed speech to remembrance and admonition; Moses tells Israel to set their hearts on his words and teach them to their children, a direct continuation of the Mosaic reminder theme.
The commentary contrasts a transient worldly life with the better lasting life; Moses calls his words no empty matter but Israel's life, giving the life claim a Mosaic scriptural counterpart.

basis: A voice heard from the middle of fire
note: Israel hears God's voice from fire but sees no form; this provides a wider Sinai form of the commentary's fire as a place of speech and revelation.

basis: Do not forget the revelation and teach it
note: Israel must guard itself from forgetting what it saw and make it known to children, directly paralleling the commentary's word gathered, not forgotten, and offered as reminder.

The commentary promises recitation without forgetting and then offers a reminder; Moses first says these words must be upon the heart, locating remembrance inwardly before the teaching practice in the next verse.

The commentary moves from recitation that is not forgotten to a reminder heard by the fearful; Moses commands Israel to repeat God's words continually and teach them to children, a concrete practice of keeping revelation present.
The commentary says the distant fire and search for guidance meet in one scene; Exodus later has God lead Israel by a pillar of fire at night, making fire explicitly a guide on the road.

basis: Fire that leads by the way
note: The night pillar of fire gives Israel light in order to travel, a concrete biblical meeting of fire, path, and divine guidance rather than fire as punishment.

basis: Write a memorial in a book and rehearse it
note: God tells Moses to write the event as a memorial in a book and place it in Joshua's hearing, directly joining Mosaic pages with remembrance and spoken teaching.
The commentary links Moses' prayer to remembrance of God's name; the altar instruction promises God's presence and blessing wherever the name is remembered in worship.

basis: Moses writes all the words of YHWH
note: Moses writes the divine words after Sinai, a direct Torah antecedent for the commentary's closing appeal to Moses's early pages.

basis: The written book of the covenant read aloud
note: Moses reads the book of the covenant to the people, bringing written pages together with recitation and hearing as in the commentary's preserved reminder.
The commentary cites Moses being chosen at the fire; Exodus sends Moses to Pharaoh from the bush, joining selection with a mission in the same encounter.

basis: Moses chosen and sent against Pharaoh
note: At the bush God sends Moses to bring Israel from Egypt, a direct counterpart to the commentary's election at the fire and its later Pharaoh scene.
The commentary links the fire encounter to prayer; God tells Moses that the people will worship God on this mountain, giving the encounter a ritual outcome.
God's sign to the commissioned Moses is that Israel will worship God at the mountain, supplying a biblical fire-to-worship movement beside the commentary's prayer after election.

The commentary places what is nearly hidden after Moses' call at the fire; Exodus answers Moses' question with God's revealed name, so the scene pairs hiddenness with disclosure rather than identifying their subjects.
At the same fire God identifies himself by name before Moses's mission; it directly accompanies the source context of Q20:14, where prayer and remembrance follow God's self-declaration.
The prose connects Moses' encounter with remembering God's name; God says the revealed name is a memorial for all generations, making name and remembrance a specific Mosaic link.
The commentary's Arabic dhikr for remembrance corresponds to Hebrew zēker in Moses' naming speech; the verse itself calls the divine name a memorial across generations.
At the bush the revealed name is God's perpetual memorial, Hebrew zikhri; its Semitic cognate relation to the commentary's li-dhikri joins divine name and remembrance at the same Moses encounter.
The prose's Moses approaches a fire that gives guidance rather than consuming him; Exodus presents the flame in the bush without consuming it, making the same fire a sign of divine presence.

basis: Moses, fire, and not being consumed
note: Exodus makes the burning bush blaze without being consumed; it supplies the same Moses-and-fire encounter against which the commentary distinguishes Moses receiving guidance near fire from the wretched person entering fire in 87:12–13.
Moses turns aside to inspect the blazing bush, giving a narrative counterpart to the commentary's distant fire that draws him into a way of guidance.
The commentary places Moses' encounter and instruction at the distant fire; in Exodus the divine voice calls Moses from the bush, so the fire scene becomes a call and response.
God calls Moses from the bush when he comes near; this is the fire-side encounter behind the commentary's sequence of fire, choice, and address.
Moses may not approach casually and must remove his sandals because the fire-side ground is holy, adding a concrete bodily response to the commentary's fire that becomes election and worship.

basis: Moses commanded to write covenant words
note: Moses is told to write the covenant words, another explicit Torah source for the commentary's final appeal to earlier Mosaic pages.
The commentary joins prayer and divine-name remembrance to Moses; after Sinai God proclaims the divine name and character before him, giving a second Mosaic setting for that conjunction.
The commentary says the person who remembers the Lord's name prays; after the name is proclaimed, Moses bows his head and worships, connecting name-revelation to embodied devotion.
Moses receives the staff with which he will perform signs, supplying the Torah's concrete bridge from the bush commission to the commentary's staff-and-magicians scene.

The commentary stresses that Moses' opponents prostrate and reject Pharaoh; Exodus has Pharaoh's magicians practice secret arts for him, so the Qur'anic conversion reverses their role in the parallel contest.
Pharaoh summons wise men and sorcerers to meet Moses, the Torah's direct setting for the commentary's later gathering of Moses, Pharaoh, and magicians.
The magicians' staffs become serpents but Aaron's staff swallows them; this supplies the contest which the commentary reads through the magicians' eventual refusal of Pharaoh.
When their art fails, the Egyptian magicians tell Pharaoh that the plague is God's finger; their recognition is a biblical counterpart to the commentary's magicians breaking with Pharaoh's claim.

The commentary presents the magicians as turning against Pharaoh and confessing God's better, lasting rule; Exodus's magicians recognize the plague as God's finger but do not renounce Pharaoh, a more limited recognition.

basis: A ruler claims divinity and is answered that he is mortal
note: The ruler of Tyre claims to sit as a god but is told he is human, a close prophetic counter-scene for the commentary's Pharaoh claiming supreme status.

basis: Arabic mar'a and Hebrew mir'eh for pasture
note: Ezekiel depicts God feeding Israel in good pasture, Hebrew mir'eh, cognate with the commentary's Arabic mar'a; it turns the shared pasture image toward sustained divine shepherding.
God sprinkles clean water, cleanses Israel, and removes its idols, giving the commentary's purification and Abrahamic distance from idolatry a single biblical cleansing horizon.
The commentary's pasture is brought out by the creator and then withers; Genesis commands the earth to bring forth seed-bearing plants and trees, grounding vegetation in divine creation.

basis: Earth commanded to bring forth vegetation
note: Creation begins with the earth bringing forth seed-bearing vegetation and fruit trees, an immediate Torah counterpart to the commentary's Creator bringing forth pasture.

basis: Melchizedek as priest of God Most High blessing Abraham
note: The priestly blessing names God Most High in an Abraham scene, supplying the canonical context for the highness title already central to the commentary's first and last images.

basis: Abraham invokes El Elyon, God Most High
note: Abraham names YHWH El Elyon, God Most High; Hebrew elyon and the commentary's al-Ala share the highness root and join the title to Abraham named in 87:19.

basis: Abraham chosen to command his household in righteousness
note: God says Abraham is known so that he will direct his household in God's way of righteousness and justice, adding a canonical Abrahamic election-and-teaching counterpart to the former-pages claim.

basis: Rain, field growth, and a worker for the ground
note: Before cultivated plants appear, the text notes both the absence of rain and of a human to work the soil, closely joining the commentary's rain, earth, body, and cultivated field.
The commentary connects divine forming with an embodied creature; Genesis says God formed the human from dust and breathed life into him, a direct creation scene joining body and ground.
God forms the human from ground and breathes life into it, furnishing the body-and-earth side of the commentary's creating and fashioning pair.

basis: Abraham keeps charge, commandments, statutes, and laws
note: Genesis attributes comprehensive obedience to Abraham, giving canonical footing for the commentary's Abrahamic former-scripture claim without assuming a canonical Abraham book.

basis: Write the vision so a reader may run
note: The vision is written plainly on tablets for a reader in motion, a specific meeting of the commentary's pages, public reminder, and path imagery.

basis: A vision for an appointed end that must be awaited
note: The vision has an appointed time and may seem slow but will come, a close prophetic analogue to the commentary's concealed decisive hour.

The commentary interprets success through a farmer's work, with a cultivated field yielding lasting good; Hosea commands sowing righteousness, reaping steadfast love, and breaking fallow ground until God sends righteousness like rain.

basis: Sow righteousness and break fallow ground
note: Hosea links cultivated ground, righteousness, and a coming divine response, a close ethical field analogue to the commentary's falah-like salvation and lasting crop.

basis: A ruler aspiring to be like the Most High
note: The arrogant ruler seeks equality with the Most High, a non-Pharaoh biblical analogue for the commentary's additional Pharaoh claim to supreme height.
Nations roar like waters but flee like chaff before wind; this joins rushing flood imagery to transient residue as the commentary does.

basis: Floodwaters sweep away a false refuge
note: Hail and overflowing waters expose a refuge made of falsehood, a prophetic water judgment that complements the commentary's flood separating what vanishes from what remains.

basis: God measures the waters and creation
note: Isaiah pictures God measuring waters in his hand and the cosmos by span, expanding the commentary's measuring scene from floodwater to ordered creation.
The commentary says the preferred worldly life is the same object as the withering pasture; Isaiah declares all flesh grass, turning that image directly toward human transience.
The commentary describes pasture drying before it is swept away; Isaiah says grass withers when the Lord's breath blows on it, giving decay a divine frame.
Isaiah's grass and flower wither under divine breath, giving a close biblical form to the commentary's worldly life becoming dried pasture.
The commentary contrasts transient worldly life with what is better and more lasting; Isaiah's grass fades but God's word stands forever, adding a specific enduring term to the contrast.

basis: God's word stands forever after grass withers
note: The word's permanence is set directly against withering grass, completing the commentary's contrast between transient vegetation and what remains.

basis: Abraham named God's friend and chosen lineage
note: Isaiah calls Israel the offspring of Abraham God's friend and the chosen servant, supporting the commentary's pairing of Abraham, election, and earlier divine promise.

basis: God guides the blind on an unknown path
note: God leads blind people on paths they do not know and turns darkness into light, a close biblical formulation for the commentary's measure-then-guidance and fire-path scene.

basis: Maker from the womb who has chosen
note: Isaiah calls God the maker and former from the womb and names the chosen servant, an unusually close pairing for the commentary's crafted body and selection.

basis: formed from the womb and creator
note: The commentary moves from bodily formation to the Lord's work in creation; Isaiah calls God the one who formed the speaker from the womb and stretched out the heavens, placing those acts under one creator.
The renewed descendants spring up among grass like trees by water, a close prophetic image for the commentary's watered growth instead of dried refuse.

basis: Refined in the furnace of affliction
note: God refines Israel in an affliction-furnace, an explicit prophetic development of the commentary's fire as corrective work rather than only punishment.

basis: The servant made a polished arrow
note: Isaiah's servant is made into a polished arrow and kept hidden; this supplies the crafted-arrow secondary sense which the commentary finds in the creation verb.
The carefully cultivated vineyard gives wild fruit instead of the expected crop; it adds a prophetic moral version of the commentary's contrast between worked land and uncontrolled growth.

basis: Fire consumes stubble because teaching is rejected
note: Fire devours stubble and dry grass because people reject God's teaching, a very close prophetic fusion of dried vegetation, fire, and refusal of reminder.

basis: Created things wear out but salvation lasts forever
note: Heavens vanish, earth wears out, and inhabitants die, while God's salvation and righteousness endure; this closely matches the commentary's temporary worldly life and better permanence.

The commentary follows water into pasture and distinguishes refuse from useful yield; Isaiah says rain waters earth so it sprouts and provides seed and bread, an especially close image of water becoming useful produce.

basis: Rain makes earth sprout and yield
note: Rain descends, waters the earth, and makes it bear seed and bread; it is the biblical side of the commentary's rain, pasture, cultivated field, and beneficial yield.
The commentary joins the rain's useful remainder to the offered reminder; Isaiah applies rain's productive return to God's word, which accomplishes its purpose rather than returning empty.

basis: The high and lofty one revives the lowly
note: The high and lofty God dwells with the contrite in order to revive them, pairing the commentary's highness with its purified, responsive person rather than the arrogant ruler.
The wicked are like a turbulent sea that throws up mire, a related prophetic water-and-waste image beside the commentary's flood-borne scum; the material correspondence is indirect.

basis: Earth and garden making righteousness and praise sprout
note: As earth makes sprouts grow, God makes righteousness and praise grow, joining the commentary's cultivated field to purification and praise.

basis: Clay, potter, and work of God's hand
note: The potter-clay image gives the commentary's craft language a biblical body-and-maker analogy without reducing it to a lexical echo.
Isaiah's final spectacle of the unquenched fire and worm that does not die is a close Hebrew-Bible horizon for the commentary's great fire and suspended death-life.
The commentary pairs the shaped creature with Moses' selection; Jeremiah says God knew and consecrated him before forming him in the womb, joining bodily formation to prophetic choice.

basis: Formed in the womb and appointed
note: Before forming Jeremiah in the womb God knows, consecrates, and appoints him; it joins formation, election, and a divine mission as the commentary does at Moses's fire.

The commentary contrasts untended growth that dries with cultivated yield; Jeremiah depicts the one who trusts in human strength as a desert shrub that does not see good, giving barrenness an ethical cause.
The commentary says the cultivated field grows and leaves a lasting share; Jeremiah's water-side tree does not cease yielding fruit even in drought, making trust the basis of endurance.

basis: No one can hide beyond God's sight
note: The prophet asks whether anyone can hide in secret places from the God who fills heaven and earth, closely matching the commentary's claim of divine knowledge of the hidden.
The divine word is likened to fire and a hammer, supporting the commentary's movement from recited reminder to a fire that actively corrects.

basis: Break fallow ground and do not sow among thorns
note: Jeremiah turns cultivation into moral exhortation, making a direct Jewish parallel for the commentary's ploughed field versus vegetation left to become waste.
The commentary's shaping image includes the embryo; Job likens God's formation of his body to milk poured and curdled, a concrete image of prenatal making.

basis: Skin, flesh, bones, and sinews fashioned
note: Job describes God clothing and knitting the body, a concrete biblical counterpart to the commentary's secondary sense of bodily and embryonic formation.
Water wears stone and sweeps away soil, a literal counterpart to the commentary's flood carrying off what has dried and become refuse.
The commentary says worldly life is also pictured as a flower and does not last; Job says a human comes forth like a flower and withers, a direct human-life use of that image.

basis: Arabic tazakka and Hebrew yizkeh around purity
note: Job asks how a human, including one born of woman, can be pure, using Hebrew yizkeh from the z-k-y root cognate with the commentary's tazakka; its setting adds bodily finitude to purification.
Job says God established weight for wind and measured the waters, closely meeting the commentary's flood running in valleys according to measure.

basis: Walking through darkness by God's lamp
note: Job recalls walking through darkness by God's shining lamp, a concrete light-and-way image alongside the commentary's fire sought for a guide.
The commentary links measured water in valleys to divine allotment; God asks who cut a channel for torrents of rain, a precise image of water given a course.
The commentary joins the valley flood to pasture; Job asks who sends rain on land where no one lives, emphasizing provision beyond human fields.
The commentary traces water to pasture's growth; Job says rain makes the wilderness satisfied and causes grass to sprout, completing that water-to-vegetation sequence.

basis: Rain makes grass sprout in waste ground
note: God's rain satisfies desolate ground and causes grass to spring up, a precise meeting of the commentary's rain-shaken earth and brought-forth pasture.

basis: Green marsh plant withering before other growth
note: A water-dependent plant withers while still green, a specific wisdom image for the commentary's pasture turning into waste; the water setting differs from its valley flood.

basis: Book in the mouth and continual meditation
note: Joshua is told not to let the Torah book depart from his mouth but to meditate on it day and night, matching the commentary's preserved speech, remembrance, and practice.

basis: Put away foreign gods and serve YHWH
note: In the Abrahamic ancestral context Joshua calls Israel to remove foreign gods and serve YHWH, a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's avoidance of idols.
Joshua's demand to choose service of YHWH or other gods makes the commentary's preference theme concrete at the point of idolatry.

The commentary closes by recalling Abraham's plea to be kept from idols; Joshua says Abraham's ancestors served other gods beyond the River, supplying the family setting from which that plea distances him.
Joshua locates Abraham's family beyond the river among worshippers of other gods, supplying canonical background for the commentary's Abrahamic plea to be kept from idols.

basis: Abraham taken from beyond the River
note: The commentary names Abraham among the recipients of the earlier pages and recalls his separation from idols; Joshua says God took Abraham from beyond the River and led him through Canaan, giving a scriptural account of his departure.
God takes Abraham from beyond the river and leads him through Canaan, matching the commentary's Abrahamic selection and its wider path-and-guidance movement.

basis: Seasonal rain producing land-yield and field fruit
note: God's rain gives land its yield and trees their fruit, a covenantal counterpart to the commentary's rain-fed field and lasting useful produce.
The commentary joins fear, remembrance, and God's name; Malachi records a book of remembrance for those who fear the Lord and esteem his name, a particularly close ethical and verbal constellation.

basis: Book of remembrance for those who fear and esteem the name
note: A book of remembrance is written for God-fearers who honor the divine name, tightly joining the commentary's reminder, fearer, name, and earlier pages.
The divine messenger sits as a refiner and purifier of silver; this gives a biblical analogue for the commentary's distinction between a fire that sets something right and a fire endured as ruin.

basis: Moses records the stages of the journey
note: Moses writes Israel's journey-stages at God's command, meeting the commentary's scrolls with its fire-and-path movement.
The proverb makes weights and measures God's work, supporting the commentary's secondary move from cosmic measuring to a just apportioned share.

basis: Furnace as testing rather than annihilation
note: The furnace tests silver and gold while God tests hearts, supplying the corrective operation of fire that the commentary sets beside fire as punishment.
The commentary links foam from fire to what is discarded while useful material remains; Proverbs says removing dross leaves workable silver, a close refining image for that distinction.

basis: Dross removed so silver becomes usable
note: Removing dross from silver leaves material for the smith, a precise counterpart to the commentary's furnace foam: what is waste departs while what is useful remains.

basis: Command as lamp and teaching as light on life's way
note: The commandment is a lamp, teaching a light, and reproofs a way of life; it joins reminder, guidance, and life in terms specific to the commentary's movement.
The commentary sets withering pasture against lasting good; Psalm 1's person who delights in instruction is a watered tree whose leaf does not wither, an enduring fruitful counterpart.

basis: Fruitful tree by streams that does not wither
note: The water-planted tree bears fruit and does not wither, concretely supplies the commentary's useful, enduring side of water and vegetation.
The commentary's dead pasture is carried off by flood; Psalm 1 says the wicked are like chaff driven by wind, using agricultural refuse for a contrasting fate.
The wicked are wind-driven chaff, a biblical residue image beside the commentary's flood-carried foam and dried pasture that do not remain.

The commentary makes the withering pasture an image for worldly life; the psalm compares human days to grass and says wind passes over it, a close mortality image without the commentary's two-field choice.

The commentary says the hereafter is better and more abiding than the world; the next psalm verse says the Lord's steadfast love lasts from everlasting to everlasting, supplying a divine permanence beside the grass image.
The commentary pictures water running through valleys and sustaining pasture; the psalm describes springs giving drink to wild animals among the mountains.
The commentary contrasts pasture with refuse and useful remainder; the psalm says God makes grass for cattle and plants for human use, specifying what the land's growth serves.

basis: God causes grass and cultivated vegetation to grow
note: The psalm distinguishes grass for animals and vegetation for human cultivation, furnishing a close biblical landscape for the commentary's pasture and worked soil.

basis: Word as lamp for foot and light for path
note: The word gives a lamp and path-light, supplying a biblical verbal-light counterpart to the commentary's fire sought as guidance.
The commentary joins craft and bodily formation; the psalm says God formed and knit the speaker in the mother's womb, making that joining explicit.
The commentary links a formed body with what is hidden; the psalm says its frame was not hidden while it was made in secret, joining bodily craft to hiddenness.
The psalm calls for praise of YHWH's name because that name alone is exalted above earth and heaven, closely meeting the commentary's name, praise, and highness.

The commentary says worldly life is a pasture that withers and is swept away; the psalm tells the faithful not to fret because evildoers quickly fade like grass, directly applying the plant image to moral outcomes.

The commentary contrasts the short-lived world with the abiding hereafter; the psalm asks the reader to mark the blameless person because his future is peace, a related lasting outcome in an ethical contrast.

The commentary pictures measured water carrying foam through valleys before useful growth remains; the psalm says God waters furrows and blesses the crop, a related but non-identical account of controlled water and yield.
The commentary opens by joining praise of the Lord's name to exalted height; this psalm closes its prayer by singing to YHWH's name as Most High, giving a close liturgical counterpart.
The commentary's al-Aʿlā and this verse's Hebrew ʿElyon are cognate Semitic forms for “Most High”; the psalm uses the title while praising YHWH's name.

The commentary treats withering pasture as the passing worldly life; the psalm says grass flourishes in the morning and fades by evening, an explicit human-time image without the commentary's later-life contrast.
The commentary opposes drying pasture to the cultivated field that keeps producing; the psalm pictures the righteous planted in God's courts, grounding the contrasting growth in worship.
The commentary says lasting good grows and leaves a remainder; the psalm says the righteous still bear fruit in old age, a pointed image of yield that persists beyond ordinary seasons.
The commentary says the preferred worldly life is the withering pasture; the psalm says the wicked sprout like grass only to be destroyed, while the righteous are later pictured as flourishing trees.

basis: A remnant refined by fire and calling God's name
note: God brings a remnant through fire, refines it, and answers when it calls the divine name, closely coupling fire, purification, name, and responsive relationship.
The commentary links measured water and the creator's measuring; Wisdom says God ordered all things by measure, number, and weight, extending that ordering to creation as a whole.

basis: All things arranged by measure, number, and weight
note: This Jewish wisdom formula directly parallels the commentary's repeated movement from measured water to a created order apportioned by God.
Wisdom presents the Egyptian magic arts as shamed during the plague darkness, a Jewish expansion of the Moses-versus-magicians setting that makes magical competence fail before God's act.
The righteous are in God's hand and no torment touches them, providing a Jewish wisdom contrast to the commentary's person destined for the great fire.

The commentary calls the hereafter better and more abiding than worldly life; Wisdom says the righteous dead are at peace and have hope full of immortality, giving that endurance a Jewish wisdom formulation.

basis: A mortal shaped in a mother's womb
note: Wisdom describes ordinary human formation in the womb from earthly mortality, a Jewish literary counterpart to the commentary's womb-to-earth connection.

basis: Abraham observed Torah before its giving
note: The Talmud reads Genesis 26:5 as Abraham's fulfillment of the whole Torah before Sinai, a major Jewish interpretation beside the commentary's Abrahamic pages.
